items.title: A searchable archive of everything
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
I wrote something down recently, and later I couldn't find it. If you know me, you know why; I put my notes into too many different apps.

Once in a while I declare loudly that "I'm using only this app, from now on! I mean it!" and then change my mind a month later. It's just the way I am. This most recent failure was the last straw and finally forced me to deal with it properly.

Instead of fixing myself, I built a software crutch. I spent today vibe-coding an indexer and search engine for all of my stuff. Here's the initial version of a web UI:

I also hacked together a TUI and an Emacs package. Those access the data via Tailscale SSH so I don't need to worry about installing things on other machines. Just the wrapper script.

Here's the list of sources being indexed (so far):

./archive index
baty.net: 1272 items (0.9s)
archive.baty.net: 2791 items (1.1s)
linux.baty.net: 26 items (0.0s)
blot.baty.net: 678 items (0.3s)
jackbaty.com: 581 items (0.1s)
notes: 2287 items (1.0s)
dayone: 2507 items (1.4s)
thebrain: 1177 items (0.5s)
mail: 1 updated, 0 removed (since revision 43773) (1.6s)
duplicates: 786 items in 381 groups (10.2s)

One nice thing about this is now I can search all of my Denote notes from my phone.

Everything is plain files and it uses boring, durable tools, so the archive should outlive whichever apps made the content that week. Even an AI layer, if I add one, sits on top of the search instead of being built into it. The database is disposable because it only takes 10 seconds to reindex everything.

Maybe now I'll be OK with all of my app churn.

items.title: Thursday, October 15, 2026
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
I swear if I hear the word "slop" one more time I'm going to punch someone in the throat.

I just did a nice and thorough de-cluttering of my office and I feel much better.

I'm tightening my requirements for people I follow. Their contribute-to-complain ratio needs to tend toward ∞.

I've started eating meals sitting at my kitchen table with no devices nearby. Sometimes I'll have a book open, but otherwise it's just me and the world. Food tastes better this way.

Have you notices that most of the entries on these daily notes start with "I..."? It bugs me sometimes, but then again, it's my blog and these are my daily notes, so

items.title: Siegler on the HomeView
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
M.G. Siegler, writing about the Apple promo video for the new HomeView:

I'm not sure I've ever felt such anxiety watching a promotional video, and certainly not one made by Apple.

I felt the same way. The video did not make me want to buy a HomeView. It made me want to go live by myself in a cabin.

items.title: Tuesday, October 13, 2026
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
I've felt a little off for a the past few days. Tired, lethargic, headache. I took an hour nap after lunch yesterday and woke up a whole new person. Felt 100%, just like that. I'll take it!

I've had a Withings scale for years. Their app has been basic, but easy to use. And by "was" I mean back then. Now, it gets worse with every update. The latest might be the final straw. There's a "Complete your profile" overlay on every screen that takes me to a permissions screen asking to allow them to send my health data to their "AI infrastructure". I'm not doing that, and I can't find a way to disable the button. On top of that, they're about to charge a $99/year subscription in order to sync my data to Apple Health. I'm definitely not paying for that. It's a bathroom scale, fer cryin' out loud.. Back to logging my weight by hand, I guess.

My grandson gets cuter and funnier every time I see him. He just turned 3, which is a great age. Right now it's all about monster trucks.

items.title: Leaning into how my brain works
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
For much of my life, I've thought that I wanted to be someone else. Or at least be a person someone else. Sometimes I'd even try to be that person. "That person" has usually been whomever I happened to be reading or watching something about. It's never worked.

Instead, maybe I shouldn't work so hard at being whatever kind of person I find interesting this week. Maybe I should be the kind of person I already am. Except, what kind even is that?

Fair question! The short answer is that I like the discovery phase of everything.

I love movies in which something strange is going on and people are trying to figure out what's happening. The problem is that I lose interest once they figure out what's happening and begin solving, killing, or running from whatever it is.

Same with video games. The games I enjoy are the open-world type where I can just walk around and explore and discover things. I don't want to be rushed, or die, or have to start over at some "save point." I only want to think, "Ooh, what's in here!?" and then see what's in there. If I get stuck somewhere for too long, I lose interest and quit.

Which brings me to my two main hobbies, photography and computers.

Computers provide an endless opportunity for exploration. There are software tools, operating systems, and nearly infinite different ways of using them. I want to try them all. This is why I do things like changing my blogging software every few months or so. I want to know what it's like to use Hugo, WordPress, Ghost, Eleventy, BSSG, Kirby, Pure Blog, and so on. It's fun setting them up, but in order to get the feel for one, I have to go all in and use it for a while. Later, once I feel like, "OK, I get it," I move to something else. Some of the time, I realize what I'm doing, but other times I come up with "reasons."

Todo apps, text editors, note-taking tools, you name it, all have the same effect on me: I want to try them. I want to see how they're configured and what it's like to use them "for real."

I spent like a year working on a transition to Linux. It was great fun, but once I felt like I'd mostly figured it out and needed to get actual work done, I kind of wanted to just fall back to macOS.

Speaking of pictures, I want to know what it's like to use a large-format film camera, or a TLR, or an ancient Barnack Leica, or whatever. What's it like to process color film at home? How does scanning negatives with a digital camera work?

Anyway, I'm beginning to understand that this is just the way I am, and I will probably always be this way. I'm never going to be that guy who always shoots film using the same camera. I'm not going to be someone who uses a 10-year-old MacBook but never thinks about trying anything else. And so on.

I'll keep trying things, getting to a point where I "get it" or get bored, and then try something else. I've always thought this was something I needed to fix, but maybe it's just who I am, and I should lean into it.
